design_detail: Narrative review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (published online 7 April 2016; May 2016 issue) by six authors from the UCL Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit, the University of Pittsburgh, the University of Exeter and The Scripps Research Institute. It covers types and potency of cannabis, acute and long-term effects on cognition, age at onset, effects after stopping, cannabis addiction (withdrawal, reward, vulnerability, treatment) and anxiety and depression, with four boxes (IQ and educational attainment; psychosis; DSM-5 cannabis use disorder; the gateway theory) and two schematic figures (CB1 receptor distribution in reward and cognition circuits; acute and chronic neurobiological changes, which the legend says should be viewed as a model). No search strategy, selection criteria, appraisal method or quantitative synthesis. 215 references, at least 19 of them with a review author as first or listed author (editors' count).
can_establish: What six cannabis psychopharmacology researchers chose in 2016 to present on cannabis and cognition, addiction and (in one box) psychosis, which primary study each figure comes from, and which questions they name as open (what level and type of use is not problematic, how repeated use affects the adolescent brain, how to treat cannabis addiction).
cannot_establish: Any causal effect or effect size of cannabis on cognition, psychosis or addiction (there is no systematic search, appraisal or pooling), and its own comparative estimate that addiction is ninefold more likely than psychosis cannot be checked, because no calculation or psychosis figure is given.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). No search method is stated. The cited evidence ranges from rodent and monkey studies and human laboratory studies (some naturalistic, in people smoking their own cannabis) to birth cohorts (Dunedin, New Zealand; a UK birth cohort; US twin cohorts), a US national survey (NESARC), European treatment data and systematic reviews.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; studies chosen by the authors.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. Cited samples as the review describes them: Dunedin cohort of 1,037 people born 1972-73, assessed at 38; UK birth cohort of 2,235 adolescents aged 15-16, born 1991-92; US twin cohort of 3,066 people aged 17-20; boys aged 13-19 with at least 200 lifetime uses (fMRI study); people aged 16-24 using cannabis daily (the authors' hair-analysis studies); European treatment entrants (mean age at first treatment 24, 83% male).
sample.selection_effects: The selection is the authors' own. At least 19 of the 215 references have a review author as first or listed author (more may be hidden behind et al.); they carry most of the human CBD evidence (refs 10, 82, 154, 181) and the acute AKT1 genotype study (ref. 177), one of the two cohort studies said to cast doubt on a causal IQ effect (Mokrysz et al., 2016, ref. 163), the potency and addiction-severity studies (Freeman et al., 2014; Freeman & Winstock, 2015) and the adolescent monkey study (Verrico et al., 2014, ref. 47), but not the main epidemiology (Dunedin, NESARC, the 2007 systematic review). Not cited: the published critique of the Dunedin IQ analysis and its reply, both in the project's Tier A list (Rogeberg, 2013; Moffitt et al., 2013), and the studies reporting deficits after 3 to 8 weeks of abstinence that a systematic review of the same year lists (Broyd et al., 2016). The psychosis box cites no genetically informed or quasi-experimental test of causation.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited studies. The review notes that studies of long-term effects rely mainly on retrospective self-report by people who choose to use cannabis, that hair analysis of THC and CBD is more objective but has limits (for example hair dye) and has rarely been used, and that all three IQ cohorts relied on self-report and none addressed potency or type of cannabis (Long-term effects, 1st paragraph, pp. 296-297; Box 1, p. 294).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Definitions differ by source and are carried in the key findings: use more than once a week (tolerance); frequent, heavy use (long-term memory deficits); at least 200 lifetime uses (fMRI study); persistent dependence (Dunedin IQ); cumulative lifetime use, with only 72 adolescents above 50 uses (UK IQ); more than 30 cumulative uses and/or daily use (US twins); regular use (psychosis, as cited from Moore et al., 2007); daily use of high-potency skunk against hash (Di Forti et al., 2015); any lifetime use (transition to dependence); daily use (withdrawal); onset before 15-17 years called early. Potency as cited: US street cannabis 4% THC in 1995 and 12% in 2014; about 15% THC with less than 0.1% CBD in Europe and Australia; cannabis supplied by NIDA for research generally under 4% THC (no citation).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol and other cognitively impairing drugs are named as confounders of long-term cognitive findings; in the UK IQ cohort, adjustment for the adolescents' cigarette and alcohol use removed the association; one cited brain-structure study compared people using cannabis daily with alcohol-matched controls (Weiland et al., 2015). Tobacco co-use is discussed as a risk factor for addiction, in combined withdrawal and as a reverse gateway to nicotine addiction.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. As cited: deficits in the first few days of abstinence but little evidence of deficits at 28 days (Crane et al., 2013); no persisting impairment beyond 4-6 weeks (Pope et al., 2001; Schreiner & Dunn, 2012); CB1 receptor availability back to control levels after about 4 weeks of monitored abstinence (Hirvonen et al., 2012) or after 2 days (D'Souza et al., 2016).

comparison.controls: Those of the cited studies: people who do not use cannabis, co-twins discordant for use, placebo in laboratory studies, alcohol-matched controls in one imaging study, the general population (one mental-health study); for transition to dependence, people who used cocaine, alcohol or tobacco.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review names cognitive ability before use as a confounder, reports which IQ cohorts measured IQ in childhood, and cites smaller orbitofrontal volume at 12 predicting use at 16 as a possible pre-existing vulnerability. For psychosis, anxiety and depression, premorbid factors appear only as a possible shared predisposition and as self-medication.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Discussed for alcohol and tobacco only.

outcomes.instruments: As in the cited studies: memory, working memory, attention, inhibition and decision-making tasks; IQ; school leaving and attainment; structural and functional MRI, DTI, and PET of CB1 receptors and dopamine synthesis; diagnoses of psychotic disorder or schizophrenia; DSM-IV dependence and DSM-5 cannabis use disorder (criteria listed in Box 3); withdrawal symptoms; self-reported depression and anxiety; anxiety disorders at 29.
outcomes.operationalization: Addiction is the authors' own construct, an acquired, chronic, relapsing disorder of strong motivation to keep using despite persistent negative consequences (p. 299); the text uses it interchangeably with DSM-IV dependence and DSM-5 cannabis use disorder. Box 3 gives DSM-5 severity as mild (2-3 criteria), moderate (4-5) and severe (6 or more), and notes that the DSM-IV legal-problems criterion was dropped. Cognitive impairment is not defined.

analysis.effect_sizes: No synthesis. Figures as cited, each with its source in the key findings: transition to dependence after any lifetime use 8.9% (cocaine 20.9%, alcohol 22.7%, tobacco 67.5%); addiction ninefold more likely than psychosis (the authors' estimate, no calculation); roughly twice the risk of psychosis with regular use; fivefold with daily skunk use (roughly threefold for any skunk use in the reference note); withdrawal in around 50% of people using daily who stop; 55% of the vulnerability to problematic use from genetic factors; IQ decline of up to 6 points (Box 1) or around 8 points (text) with persistent dependence; no IQ association in the UK and US cohorts; no persisting cognitive impairment beyond 4-6 weeks of abstinence; cocaine use among people who had used cannabis 22% in the Netherlands and 33% in the US.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection (see selection effects). Where a source's wording differs from the review's (schizophrenia for psychotic disorder; addiction for dependence or problematic use; daily for frequent use), the review's own wording is printed in the text; see reporting issues.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As a narrative review it reports no new data. The evidence it cites shows: acute THC impairs working and episodic memory dose-dependently in laboratory studies; long-term deficits are reported mainly with frequent, heavy use and are hard to separate from confounding; two cited sources report no persisting impairment beyond 4-6 weeks of abstinence, and CB1 receptor availability normalises within 2 days to 4 weeks; of three prospective IQ cohorts, one (Dunedin) reports decline with persistent dependence and two with lighter exposure (UK; US twins) report no association after adjustment or within discordant twin pairs; regular use goes with roughly twice the risk of psychosis (Moore et al., 2007) and daily high-potency use with higher odds of psychotic disorder in one case-control study (Di Forti et al., 2015); 8.9% of people who ever use cannabis are estimated to develop DSM-IV dependence over their lifetime (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract is restrained: it calls addiction a much more common problem than psychosis and says the causality and longevity of cognitive changes are fiercely debated (p. 293). The gaps are in the body. (1) Recovery is stated as a convergence of evidence, "converging to show that cognitive impairments do not persist beyond 4–6 weeks after abstinence" (p. 298), on two cited sources, with receptor normalisation offered as further support although receptor availability is not cognitive performance; the Dunedin finding the review itself reports (decline still apparent in people using less than weekly at 38, Box 1) is not set against it. (2) The ninefold comparison of addiction with psychosis (p. 298) is the authors' estimate from three sources with no calculation or psychosis figure shown. (3) The Dunedin decline is around 8 IQ points in the text (p. 298) and up to 6 in Box 1 (p. 294). (4) Box 2 asks whether cannabis is cause, consequence or correlate of psychosis, but its later paragraphs speak of how cannabis increases the risk of psychosis and of its pro-psychotic impact, and it turns a first-episode psychosis case-control estimate into a fivefold chance of having schizophrenia. (5) The closing policy views (cannabis might be judged comparatively benign; a carefully regulated market might reduce harms; p. 303) are opinion without cited evidence. Against this, the Conclusions say plainly that evidence of clear causality is lacking (p. 302).

timeline.event: Fergusson et al. (2003), ref. 166: the association between early school leaving and later cannabis use was accounted for by cannabis use before leaving school; the only test of reverse causation for education that the review cites (Box 1).
Lynskey et al. (2003), ref. 190, co-twin study: escalation to other drugs in early-onset cannabis use not attributable to shared genetic or environmental factors alone (Box 4).
Systematic review cited for roughly twice the risk of psychosis with regular use and for more mixed evidence on depression and anxiety (ref. 62)
NESARC analysis cited for the 8.9% transition from first use to dependence (ref. 64)
Meier et al. (2012), ref. 54, Dunedin cohort: IQ decline with persistent cannabis dependence (up to 6 points in Box 1, around 8 in the text).
Hirvonen et al. (2012), ref. 30, PET: cortical CB1 receptor downregulation in daily use, correlated with years of use, back to control levels after about 4 weeks of monitored abstinence.

Cheetham et al. (2012), ref. 49: smaller orbitofrontal volume at 12 predicted cannabis use at 16, which the review reads as a possible vulnerability factor rather than a consequence (a test of reverse causation for brain structure).

Grant et al. (2012), ref. 175, and Verweij et al. (2013), ref. 170, co-twin control analyses: no difference in years of education or early school leaving within twin pairs discordant for cannabis use (Box 1).
Rogeberg (2013), published critique of the Dunedin IQ analysis (socioeconomic confounding), and the reply by Moffitt et al. (2013): both in the project's Tier A list; neither is cited by this review.
Di Forti et al. (2015), ref. 180, south London case-control study of first-episode psychosis: daily skunk use and psychotic disorder (fivefold), hash not associated (Box 2).

Weiland et al. (2015), ref. 158: no brain morphometric differences between people using cannabis daily and alcohol-matched controls; listed in the project's Tier B list as a non-replication of Gilman et al. (2014).

Mokrysz et al. (2016, ref. 163, a review author's study), UK birth cohort, and Jackson et al. (2016, ref. 164), US twin cohorts: no IQ association after adjustment for pre-teen IQ and confounders (in particular the adolescents' cigarette and alcohol use), and none within discordant twin pairs; the review reads both as casting doubt on a causal effect, with fewer exposures than in Dunedin.
Systematic review of 2004-2015 task-based studies published the same year: persistence after abstinence rated mixed for memory and attention, with deficits in some studies at 3 to 8 weeks

replication.where_it_stands: A widely cited overview whose figures are all second-hand: the dependence figures come from Lopez-Quintero et al. (2011; the project's card sc_lopez_quintero_2011 gives 8.9% as the lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV dependence among people who used cannabis), the psychosis risk from Moore et al. (2007), the recovery window from Pope et al. (2001) and Schreiner & Dunn (2012), and the IQ evidence from Meier et al. (2012), Mokrysz et al. (2016) and Jackson et al. (2016). The genetically informed tests of the psychosis association in the project's Tier A list (the Mendelian randomization studies of 2017-2018; Gillespie & Kendler, 2021) and the later co-twin and meta-analytic studies of cognition (Meier et al., 2018; Scott et al., 2018) post-date it. Claims should cite the primary studies and use this review for its arguments and the open questions it names.

funding.funder: US National Institutes of Health grants to L.H.P. (AA020404, AA006420, AA022249 and AA017447); UK Medical Research Council grants to H.V.C. and C.J.A.M. (G0800268; MR/K015524/1) (Acknowledgements, p. 306).
funding.declared_conflicts: Competing interests statement as printed: the authors declare competing interests, with the details given only in the web version (p. 306). The web version is not on file, so what the interests are was not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Curran, Freeman, Mokrysz and Morgan: Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit, University College London (Morgan also University of Exeter); Lewis: Department of Psychiatry, University of Pittsburgh; Parsons: The Scripps Research Institute. Much of the CBD, potency, hair-analysis and UK IQ evidence cited is the authors' own (see selection effects). The declared competing interests could not be read. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that test cognition before any cannabis use and repeatedly afterwards (as the review says the ABCD Study is designed to do), with biologically verified exposure including THC and CBD content, testing after verified abstinence of several lengths, co-twin or sibling comparisons and full adjustment for alcohol, tobacco and other drugs; and, for the comparison of addiction with psychosis, the lifetime incidence of both outcomes estimated in the same cohort of people who use cannabis.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; the authors chose the evidence.

Limits are named for some studies (light exposure in the UK IQ cohort; only 47 frequent-use discordant twin pairs in the US study; reliance on self-report; cross-sectional imaging with differing abstinence and confounds; heterogeneity in the 43-study imaging review), but the sources of the headline figures are given without their designs: the 4-6 weeks recovery statement, the twofold psychosis risk and the skunk estimate; the ninefold comparison is not derived.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: At least 19 of 215 references; they carry most of the human CBD evidence, one of the two cohort studies cited against a causal IQ effect, the potency studies and the adolescent monkey study, but not the main epidemiology.

The mechanistic figure is labelled a model and the potency-treatment link is called possible; but the ninefold estimate is presented without method, several statements carry no citation (intoxication lasting about 5-120 minutes when smoked; nearly 2,000 studies on psychosis since 1962; most people rating benefits above risks; research funding aimed at harms; cannabis rarely kills), and the closing policy views sit beside the evidence.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on lasting cognitive effects and on causation (evidence of deficits persisting after weeks of abstinence, and non-causal explanations of the psychosis association, under-represented)
domains.note: For IQ both readings are given (Dunedin against the UK and US cohorts) and educational attainment is treated as likely confounded. Recovery within 4-6 weeks is stated as convergent without the abstinence studies that report deficits at 3 to 8 weeks; the psychosis box gives the twofold risk, the vulnerability-genotype studies and the skunk study, and notes that most people who use cannabis never develop psychosis, but does not discuss reverse causation, shared genetic liability or population trends in schizophrenia.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The selection is the authors' own and unsystematic, the headline figures come from cited primary studies or from an uncomputed estimate, and evidence on lasting effects and on causation is unevenly represented; on the other hand the review says explicitly that causality is debated and that clear causal evidence is lacking. It may be cited for its arguments, for the open questions it names and as a pointer to primary studies; each figure should be cited from its primary source (named in the key findings), and the ninefold comparison should not be used as a sourced estimate.

key_findings.finding: People using cannabis worldwide are put at 182 million (United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, World Drug Report 2015, ref. 5).
key_findings.locator: Introduction (untitled), 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand. Broyd et al. (2016) give 178 million from three other sources, including the 2014 edition of the same report.

key_findings.finding: Potency, as cited: the THC content of US street cannabis rose from 4% in 1995 to 12% in 2014 (ElSohly et al., 2016, ref. 15); high-potency cannabis with about 15% THC and less than 0.1% CBD now dominates the markets of Europe (Hardwick & King, 2008; Niesink et al., 2015) and Australia (Swift et al., 2013), while CBD content has fallen to negligible levels. The review states, without a citation, that cannabis supplied by NIDA for research generally has less than 4% THC, and argues that older cohort studies such as the New Zealand birth cohort are of limited relevance to cannabis used today.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis: a plant with many forms, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures; the NIDA figure has no citation.

key_findings.finding: Acute effects: a single dose of cannabis or THC impairs working and episodic memory, dose-dependently (Curran et al., 2002, a study by the first author, ref. 24; Crane et al., 2013, review, ref. 25); encoding of new memories is impaired while retrieval of memories consolidated when not intoxicated is not, and working-memory deficits concern manipulating more than holding information (these two statements without citation); THC prevents the load-related rise in dorsolateral prefrontal activity (Bossong et al., 2012). The intoxication period is put at about 5-120 minutes when smoked, without a citation. Findings on attention, decision-making and risk-taking are called mixed and task dependent (refs 25, 27). Tolerance to the memory and psychomotor effects is reported in people who use cannabis more than once a week (D'Souza et al., 2008; Ramaekers et al., 2011), probably through CB1 receptor downregulation.
key_findings.locator: Cognition, learning and memory › Acute effects, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: CBD: smoking cannabis with more CBD protected people who use cannabis regularly against the acute memory impairment from THC (Morgan et al., 2010, ref. 10, a study by review authors), replicated in volunteers who used cannabis (Englund et al., 2013, ref. 11); CBD alone enhanced fear-extinction learning (Das et al., 2013); a cross-sectional hair-analysis study found smaller hippocampal volume with chronic THC exposure but not in people with CBD as well as THC in hair, nor after extended abstinence (Yücel et al., 2016, ref. 33). The review calls for research on whether chronic CBD exposure protects in the longer term.
key_findings.locator: Cognition, learning and memory › Acute effects, 4th paragraph (p. 295, continuing on p. 296); note to reference 33 (p. 304)

key_findings.finding: Long-term effects: studies rely mainly on retrospective self-report by people who choose to use cannabis; long-term memory impairments have been reported mainly with frequent, heavy use, and confounding (cognitive ability before use; alcohol and other drugs; type of cannabis; age at onset; depression and cannabis addiction) makes cause and effect hard to establish. Case-control studies are called inconsistent; the most consistent finding is impaired encoding of new episodic memories, with persisting deficits in some studies over the first few days of abstinence but little evidence of persisting deficits at 28 days (as summarised by Crane et al., 2013, ref. 25); working memory, attention and impulsivity findings are mixed. One study found no difference in decision making or risk taking against controls matched for mental-health confounders, but poorer decision-making accuracy went with more cannabis addiction symptoms (Gonzalez et al., 2012, ref. 35).
key_findings.locator: Long-term effects, 1st paragraph (pp. 296-297) and 2nd paragraph (p. 297)

key_findings.finding: Imaging: a systematic review of 43 studies (Batalla et al., 2013, ref. 36) is cited as concluding that chronic cannabis use may alter brain structure and function, with remarkable heterogeneity, mainly cross-sectional designs and no possible causal inference; deficits are said to be most consistent only with heavy use, the group most likely to have cannabis addiction. The authors propose that cognitive changes may interact with genetic vulnerability to raise the risk of addiction.
key_findings.locator: Long-term effects, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Preclinical, as cited: repeated THC impairs working memory, object recognition and prepulse inhibition more in adolescent than in adult rodents (refs 40-43); in adolescent monkeys given THC for 6 months, at doses the review equates with human self-administration (about 1-2 joints on 5 days a week), the usual improvement on a spatial working-memory task was blunted but not that on an object working-memory task (Verrico et al., 2014, ref. 47, from a review author's group).
key_findings.locator: Age-dependent effects: adolescence and adulthood, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Animal data; the dose equivalence is the review's statement, reported here only as the study condition.

key_findings.finding: Adolescence in humans: evidence that cognition and brain structure are more disrupted when use starts in adolescence is called accumulating but with few direct comparisons with adult onset. Smaller orbitofrontal volume at 12 predicted cannabis use at 16, which the review reads as a possible vulnerability factor rather than a consequence (Cheetham et al., 2012, ref. 49); smaller hippocampal volume relates less consistently to age at onset than to amount of use (Lorenzetti et al., 2014, ref. 50). Boys aged 13-19 with at least 200 lifetime uses showed more prefrontal activation during a working-memory task than age-matched controls (Jager et al., 2010, ref. 51). Adolescent onset is reported to go with greater deficits in visuospatial attention (Ehrenreich et al., 1999) and in verbal fluency and inhibition (Gruber et al., 2012) than adult onset. The Dunedin analysis is described here as cannabis addiction starting in adolescence and persisting into adulthood being associated with a decline of around 8 IQ points (Meier et al., 2012, ref. 54), with two recent large studies said to cast doubt on a causal explanation. Early onset is defined by age (before 15-17 years) rather than by pubertal stage; one study found younger age of regular use associated with poorer memory in women but not men, and earlier initiation with better decision-making in both (Crane et al., 2015, ref. 56).
key_findings.locator: Age-dependent effects: adolescence and adulthood, 4th paragraph (p. 297); 6th, 7th and 8th paragraphs (p. 298)
key_findings.note: Box 1 gives the same Dunedin decline as up to 6 IQ points (p. 294); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Box 1, IQ: three large prospective cohorts. New Zealand (Dunedin) birth cohort of 1,037 people born 1972-73 and assessed at 38: persistent cannabis dependence was associated with a decline of up to 6 IQ points from the IQ measured at 7-13, most evident when dependence began in adolescence and still apparent in people using less than once a week at 38 (Meier et al., 2012, ref. 54). UK birth cohort of 2,235 adolescents aged 15-16, born 1991-92: cumulative cannabis use was not associated with lower IQ than in controls who did not use cannabis once pre-teen IQ and confounders, in particular the adolescents' cigarette and alcohol use, were taken into account, but only 72 reported more than 50 lifetime uses (Mokrysz et al., 2016, ref. 163, a review author's study). US twin cohort of 3,066 people aged 17-20: no IQ difference from the IQ measured at 9-12 within monozygotic or dizygotic pairs discordant for use, but only 47 discordant pairs in which the twin who used did so frequently (more than 30 cumulative uses and/or daily) (Jackson et al., 2016, ref. 164). The review concludes that the UK and US studies suggest genetic or environmental factors drive the association, while noting their younger participants and fewer exposures; it adds that all three relied on retrospective self-report, ignored possible residual drug effects on testing and did not address potency.
key_findings.locator: Box 1, Does cannabis affect IQ?, paragraphs 1-6
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures. The adjustment sets are as summarised by the review; take them from the primary papers before citing.

key_findings.finding: Box 1, education: associations of adolescent cannabis use with early school leaving and poorer educational performance are called fairly consistent (refs 166-169) and typically robust to adjustment for early-life factors, baseline school performance or ability, disadvantage and parental education (refs 167, 169). The one test of reverse causation found that the association between early school leaving and later cannabis use was accounted for by cannabis use before leaving school (Fergusson et al., 2003, ref. 166). Adjusting for teenage use of other substances attenuated the association with attainment (refs 163, 173, 174), and twin pairs discordant for cannabis use did not differ in early school leaving (Verweij et al., 2013, ref. 170) or years of education (Grant et al., 2012, ref. 175), which the review takes as strong support for unmeasured confounding. A PET study linked lower striatal dopamine synthesis in people who use cannabis to a measure of amotivation (Bloomfield et al., 2014, ref. 171, with review authors).
key_findings.locator: Box 1, Does cannabis use affect educational attainment?, paragraphs 1-5

key_findings.finding: After stopping: the review states that studies of long-term effects after stopping are "converging to show that cognitive impairments do not persist beyond 4–6 weeks after abstinence", citing two sources (Pope et al., 2001, ref. 58; Schreiner & Dunn, 2012, ref. 59). As further support it cites PET: cortical CB1 receptor downregulation in people using cannabis chronically, correlated with years of use, returned to control levels after about 4 weeks of continuously monitored abstinence on a secure research unit (Hirvonen et al., 2012, ref. 30), and after as little as 2 days in one study (D'Souza et al., 2016, ref. 31); reversible downregulation is also shown in rodents. Imaging studies of persisting effects are called cross-sectional, with differing abstinence intervals and confounds (comorbid alcohol use; functioning before cannabis) that prevent causal conclusions; longitudinal studies are called for, including in people who start in adolescence (citing Fried et al., 2005).
key_findings.locator: Effects persisting after stopping use, paragraph (single paragraph)
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the receptor findings concern CB1 availability, not cognitive performance. The abstinence intervals and tests of the two sources are not given.

key_findings.finding: Box 2, psychosis: several longitudinal, population-based studies are said to show an earlier first episode (Large et al., 2011, ref. 176, a meta-analysis) and a roughly twofold increase in the risk of psychosis with regular cannabis use (Moore et al., 2007, ref. 62). The box notes, without citation, that the vast majority of people who use cannabis do not develop psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia and that many people with these disorders have never used cannabis. It describes more agreement that heavy use may lead young people vulnerable to psychosis to develop the disorder, with AKT1 genotype studies cited for a genetic basis (Morgan et al., 2016, ref. 177, by review authors; Di Forti et al., 2012; van Winkel et al., 2011). Self-reported hash use, even daily, is said not to be associated with increased risk, while daily use of skunk (high THC, negligible CBD) is associated with a fivefold greater chance of having schizophrenia (Di Forti et al., 2015, ref. 180); studies with biological markers of use show CBD reducing the psychosis-like effects of THC (refs 154 and 181, both by review authors). Mechanisms are called unclear (reduced dopamine release in people who use cannabis, ref. 116; anandamide and CB1 receptor findings in schizophrenia). The box also states, without citation, that nearly 2,000 studies on the topic have been published since 1962.
key_findings.locator: Box 2, paragraphs 1-5
key_findings.note: The reference note for Di Forti et al. (2015) on p. 306 gives the outcome as psychotic disorder, roughly threefold for skunk use and fivefold for daily skunk use compared with people who did not use cannabis; see reporting issues. The twofold figure is second-hand from Moore et al. (2007), and no exposure definition or adjustment set is given for it.

key_findings.finding: Addiction against psychosis: the authors write "we estimate that people who try cannabis are ninefold more likely to become addicted" to it than to develop psychosis in their lifetime, citing Moore et al. (2007), Kessler et al. (1994, National Comorbidity Survey) and Lopez-Quintero et al. (2011) (refs 62-64). No calculation and no lifetime psychosis figure are given.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis addiction, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The authors' own estimate, not a figure reported by any of the three sources; it cannot be reproduced from this paper.

key_findings.finding: Dependence after use: the estimated chance of becoming addicted to cannabis after lifetime exposure is given as 8.9%, against 20.9% for cocaine, 22.7% for alcohol and 67.5% for tobacco (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011, ref. 64). DSM-5 merged the DSM-IV categories of cannabis abuse and dependence into cannabis use disorder (Box 3). The need for treatment is called substantial and increasing in North America, Europe and Oceania (UNODC, 2015), and across Europe cannabis accounts for more first-time entrants to drug treatment than any other illicit drug (EMCDDA, 2015, ref. 70).
key_findings.locator: Cannabis addiction › Cannabis addiction and withdrawal, 1st paragraph; Box 3
key_findings.note: Second-hand. The source's construct, by its title, is transition from first use to DSM-IV dependence; the project's card sc_lopez_quintero_2011 records 8.9% as the lifetime cumulative probability of transition to DSM-IV dependence among people who used cannabis, without confidence intervals. The review's word addicted should not be carried into claims.

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal: a cannabis withdrawal syndrome affects around 50% of people using daily when they stop, typically begins 1-2 days after stopping, peaks at 2-6 days and remits at 1-2 weeks (Budney et al., 2004, review, ref. 71); prominent symptoms are craving, sleep problems, nightmares, anger, irritability, dysphoria and nausea (Allsop et al., 2011, ref. 72). Symptoms correlate with reduced CB1 receptor availability in acute abstinence (D'Souza et al., 2016) and can be alleviated by THC in a dose-dependent manner, citing one study of oral THC (Budney et al., 2007, ref. 73, by its title); in people using both cannabis and tobacco daily, combined withdrawal is stronger than withdrawal from either alone (Vandrey et al., 2008, ref. 77).
key_findings.locator: Cannabis addiction and withdrawal, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Potency, CBD and reward: cannabis with more THC (3.5% against 2.0%) produced stronger reinforcement in human choice studies (as reviewed by Justinova et al., 2005, ref. 78), but the review says this is hard to extrapolate to cannabis with about 15% THC; people adapt to stronger cannabis by putting less in joints (Freeman et al., 2014, ref. 79, review authors) and/or inhaling less smoke (van der Pol et al., 2014, ref. 80); cross-sectional data link high-THC cannabis with greater addiction severity (Freeman & Winstock, 2015, ref. 81, review authors), and the review calls it possible that rising potency contributed to rising demand for treatment. People smoking low-CBD cannabis showed more attentional capture by cannabis cues than people smoking high-CBD cannabis (Morgan et al., 2010, ref. 82, review authors), but CBD does not alter the acute reinforcing effects or the rewarding feeling of being stoned (refs 82, 84, 85). Synthetic CB1 agonists are described as less addictive than natural cannabis, with more negative effects, and preferred by only 7% (Winstock & Barratt, 2013, ref. 93).
key_findings.locator: Cannabinoids and reward, 1st paragraph (p. 299); 2nd and 4th paragraphs (p. 300)

key_findings.finding: Box 4, gateway: evidence is said to support sequential progression and an association between cannabis and other illicit drugs, increasing with frequency of use and adolescent onset (Fergusson et al., 2006, ref. 189), and a twin study suggested this is not attributable to shared genetic or environmental factors alone (Lynskey et al., 2003, ref. 190); the review states that establishing causality remains difficult and mechanisms speculative. Cocaine use among people who have used cannabis is given as 22% in the Netherlands and 33% in the United States (MacCoun & Reuter, 2001, ref. 195). Smoking tobacco with cannabis is described as a possible route to nicotine addiction, a reverse gateway (refs 160, 199).
key_findings.locator: Box 4, paragraphs 1-4

key_findings.finding: Vulnerability: only a minority of people who use cannabis become addicted. Concurrent tobacco use (refs 128-130), early adolescent onset and frequent, especially daily, use (Coffey et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2005) are cited as risk factors; males have earlier opportunity to use, greater risk and faster progression (refs 64, 128, 129). European treatment data: mean age at first treatment 24, mean age at first use 16, 83% of people treated male (EMCDDA, 2015, ref. 70). A 3-year prospective study found that variables directly related to cannabis use did not predict transition to addiction, whereas living alone, coping motives and negative life events did (van der Pol et al., 2013, ref. 215). A meta-analysis of 24 twin studies attributed 55% of the vulnerability to genetic influences, 17.5% to shared and 27.5% to non-shared environment (Verweij et al., 2010, ref. 132).
key_findings.locator: Vulnerability factors, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand. The review calls the van der Pol sample people who used daily, while the reference title speaks of frequent use; the twin meta-analysis is titled as concerning cannabis use initiation and problematic use, which the review renders as addiction. The project's card sc_lopez_quintero_2011 records that, in that survey, early onset (before 14) predicted transition to cannabis dependence before adjustment but went with a lower hazard after adjustment (hazard ratio 0.63).

key_findings.finding: Treatment: no pharmacotherapy is approved; a 12-week trial of gabapentin (Mason et al., 2012, ref. 137) and an 8-week trial of N-acetylcysteine (Gray et al., 2012, ref. 138) showed promise for reducing use by urine testing; dronabinol (Levin et al., 2011) and nabiximols (Allsop et al., 2014) reduced withdrawal symptoms and improved retention but did not reduce use compared with placebo. Cannabis addiction is described as not easily treated by psychological therapies (Cooper et al., 2015, ref. 135).
key_findings.locator: Possible treatments for cannabis addiction, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Anxiety and depression: the evidence for an association of regular use with anxiety and depression is called more mixed and less consistent than for psychosis (Moore et al., 2007). In one study comparing people who used cannabis frequently with and without DSM-IV dependence, only those with dependence had depression and anxiety problems; those without dependence differed from the general population only in more externalizing disorders, likely to predate their use (van der Pol et al., 2013, ref. 145). In the authors' own study of people aged 16-24 who used daily, THC in hair was associated with self-reported depression and anxiety (Morgan et al., 2012, ref. 154). An epidemiological study cited as ref. 146 found no consistent association between adolescent use and depression at 29, but more than double the rate of anxiety disorders at 29 with daily use or addiction in early adulthood, compared with people who did not use cannabis; the review offers shared predisposition and self-medication of social anxiety (refs 155, 156) as explanations.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis, anxiety and depression, 1st paragraph (pp. 301-302) and 3rd paragraph (p. 302)
key_findings.note: Ref. 146 as printed is a 2003 paper on cannabis and psychosis; the source of the age-29 figures cannot be identified from the paper (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: evidence of clear causality is lacking, but the undesired effects may range from mild cognitive impairment to disabling psychiatric disorders; problems are seen mainly with heavy, frequent use, and the level and type of use that is not problematic is unknown; one study found no brain-structure differences between people using cannabis daily with alcohol and alcohol-matched controls (Weiland et al., 2015, ref. 158); people with schizophrenia who use cannabis had better cognition than those who do not in a meta-analysis (Yücel et al., 2012, ref. 159); rising prevalence of cannabis use disorder in the US is cited (Hasin et al., 2015, ref. 161). The ABCD Study (10,000 children from age 9-10, followed 10 years) is named as the needed design, without citation. The authors' closing views are that cannabis, which rarely kills people, might well be judged comparatively benign, and that a carefully regulated market might increase control over age of initiation and the availability of lower-THC, higher-CBD cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions and future directions, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 302); 4th paragraph (pp. 302-303); 5th and 6th paragraphs (p. 303)

key_findings.finding: Funding: US National Institutes of Health grants to Parsons and UK Medical Research Council grants to Curran and Morgan. The competing interests statement says the authors declare competing interests and refers to the web version for details.
key_findings.locator: Acknowledgements; Competing interests statement

reporting_issues.issue: The Dunedin decline is reported as up to 6 IQ points with persistent cannabis dependence in Box 1 (p. 294) and as around 8 IQ points with cannabis addiction starting in adolescence and persisting into adulthood in the text (p. 298), both citing Meier et al. (2012, ref. 54) and the text referring to Box 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: The same finding appears with two magnitudes and two exposure definitions; Broyd et al. (2016) give about 6 points. Take the figure, exposure group and comparison from Meier et al. (2012) itself.

reporting_issues.issue: Box 2 states that daily skunk use is associated with a fivefold greater chance of having schizophrenia, while the note to the same reference (Di Forti et al., 2015, ref. 180), titled as a study of first-episode psychosis, gives the outcome as psychotic disorder, roughly threefold for any skunk use and fivefold for daily skunk use compared with people who did not use cannabis.
reporting_issues.consequence: The outcome is mislabelled in the box: claims must say psychotic disorder (first-episode psychosis case-control), not schizophrenia, and should take the estimate and its comparison group from the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Ref. 146 is printed as Degenhardt, Hall and Lynskey (2003), titled as testing hypotheses about the relationship between cannabis use and psychosis, but is cited for a recent epidemiological study of depression and anxiety disorders at age 29 and for depression and anxiety being associated with cannabis addiction.
reporting_issues.consequence: The source of the age-29 findings (no consistent association with depression; more than double the rate of anxiety disorders) cannot be identified from the paper; they should not be cited from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The ninefold estimate that people who try cannabis are more likely to become addicted than to develop psychosis is given without a calculation or the lifetime psychosis figure used, and is attributed to three sources jointly (refs 62-64).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure cannot be reproduced or checked; it is an estimate by the authors, and its comparison mixes a lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV dependence among people who used cannabis with a psychosis risk of unstated origin.

reporting_issues.issue: The same study (Bloomfield et al., 2014, ref. 116) is described as showing reduced dopamine release in people who use cannabis (Box 2, p. 298) and as showing reduced capacity to synthesize striatal dopamine, driven by people meeting criteria for cannabis use disorder (p. 301; Figure 2 legend, p. 296).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; release and synthesis capacity are different measures, and the mechanistic argument in Box 2 rests on the description that differs from the text.

reporting_issues.issue: Box 1 calls all three IQ studies prospective cohort studies but says that all relied on retrospective self-report of cannabis use, without explaining in what sense the reports were retrospective.
reporting_issues.consequence: The measurement critique cannot be checked from the review; exposure measurement should be taken from the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: Several statements carry no citation: intoxication lasting about 5-120 minutes when smoked (p. 295); research cannabis from NIDA generally below 4% THC (p. 294); nearly 2,000 studies on cannabis and psychosis since 1962 and the statement that many people with psychotic disorders never used cannabis (Box 2, p. 298); most people who use cannabis recreationally or medically rating benefits above risks and research funding being aimed at harms (p. 302); the ABCD Study design and cannabis rarely killing people (p. 303).
reporting_issues.consequence: None of these can be cited from this review as evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: Constructs shift between the review and its sources: DSM-IV dependence (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011, by title) and problematic use (Verweij et al., 2010, by title) are reported as addiction, and a study titled as concerning frequent use (van der Pol et al., 2013, ref. 215) is described as a study of daily use.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims must use the source's exposure and outcome definitions, not the review's wording.

reporting_issues.issue: Box 1 says that all three prospective IQ studies ignored possible residual effects of cannabis on IQ test performance, gives the New Zealand cohort as 1,037 38-year-olds, and reports only the within-pair result of the US twin study. Meier et al. (2012) left out people who had used cannabis in the day or the week before testing in sensitivity analyses (Fig. 1), analysed 874 members (1,037 is the birth cohort), and the US study (Jackson et al., 2016) also reports a between-family decline in Vocabulary that the box does not mention.
reporting_issues.consequence: The box's measurement critique does not hold for Dunedin as stated, and the box cannot be cited for the Dunedin analytic sample or for the US twin study's overall finding; take these from the primary papers.

The web version holding the details of the declared competing interests is not on file; there is no supplementary material.

disagreements.first_pass: Withdrawal: a cannabis withdrawal syndrome affects around 50% of people using daily when they stop, typically begins 1-2 days after stopping, peaks at 2-6 days and remits at 1-2 weeks (Budney et al., 2004, review, ref. 71); prominent symptoms are craving, sleep problems, nightmares, anger, irritability, dysphoria and nausea (Allsop et al., 2011, ref. 72). Symptoms correlate with reduced CB1 receptor availability in acute abstinence (D'Souza et al., 2016) and are relieved by THC in a dose-dependent manner (Budney et al., 2007, ref. 73); in people using both cannabis and tobacco daily, combined withdrawal is stronger than withdrawal from either alone (Vandrey et al., 2008, ref. 77).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 213, corrected: Curran says withdrawal symptoms 'can be alleviated by THC in a dose-dependent manner' (p. 299), citing one study of oral THC (ref. 73); 'are relieved' is stronger than the source. The rest of the finding is confirmed.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 299 in the PDF text and reference 73 (titled as a study in which oral THC suppresses withdrawal symptoms). Wording brought back to the source's hedge; reported as the review's statement of a laboratory finding, not as advice.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 213, missed (three items on Box 1, p. 294): the residual-effects statement is not accurate for Dunedin; 1,037 is the cohort, not the number analysed; only the within-pair result of the US twin study is reported.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading Box 1 in the PDF text (p. 294) against Meier et al. (2012; saved PMC text: Results › Is Impairment Attributable..., 1st paragraph and Fig. 1 legend, exclusion of past-24-hour and past-week use; Table 1, 874) and Jackson et al. (2016; Table 3). Combined into one reporting issue.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 213: would rate the gap substantial rather than minor (recovery within 4-6 weeks stated as converging on two sources, a fivefold chance of schizophrenia from a first-episode case-control estimate, an uncomputed ninefold estimate); calls it a judgment call.
disagreements.resolution: Not changed: a difference of judgment on the interpretation-gap rating, which METHODS §5.5 leaves to the senior author; listed for him in the adjudication log.
